implementation_notes: Rails ships pessimistic row locking: Model.lock.find(id), record.lock!(clause) and record.with_lock { ... }, which wraps the block in a transaction and reloads the record with a lock (the API notes that lock! raises when the record has unsaved changes). The lock is released when the transaction ends, so the offline lease is a lock record claimed inside one short transaction, with a PostgreSQL advisory lock or a lock table as the storage. The classic structure remains because with_lock cannot span the several requests that make up one business transaction.
code_sketch:
Order.transaction do
  lock = LockRecord.lock.find_by(lockable: key)   # SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
  raise Locked.new(lock.owner) if lock && lock.owner != session_id
  LockRecord.create!(lockable: key, owner: session_id,
                     acquired_at: Time.now.utc) unless lock
end
pitfalls: lock! reloads the record and raises when it has unsaved changes (and ActiveRecord::ReadOnlyError when writes are being prevented) - commit or reload before locking instead of wrapping a dirty object.
Pessimistic locks only mean something inside a transaction; Rails releases the row lock at commit, so code that calls lock! outside one holds nothing by the next request.
The connection pool is per thread: a lock taken inside a request's transaction cannot be carried into the next request, which is exactly why the owner/timeout record exists.
